title: Psalm 41: Betrayed by a Friend; Book I Closes
summary: The psalm begins by blessing the one who cares for the poor, promising that the LORD will sustain him in sickness. The speaker, himself ill, confesses his sin and asks for healing while enemies wait for him to die and even a trusted friend who ate his bread turns against him. He asks God to raise him up, trusts that God upholds him, and the psalm ends with the doxology that closes Book I of the Psalter.
story: Psalm 41 is the last psalm of Book I (Psalms 1 to 41). It closes with a blessing of the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting, and a double Amen, a formula that marks the end of each of the Psalter's first four books (see 72:18-19, 89:52, and 106:48). Book I opened in Psalm 1 with the word blessed for the one who delights in God's law, and Psalm 41 opens with the same word for the one who cares for the poor, so the collection is framed by blessing. The psalm also carries a line that Jesus applied to Judas at the Last Supper, which gives it a prominent place in the Gospel story.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David and directs it to the choirmaster. No occasion is named. Many readers connect the betrayal of verse 9 with Ahithophel, David's trusted counselor, who joined Absalom's rebellion against him (2 Samuel 15:12, 31; 16:23). Others see the psalm as a prayer used in the temple by any sick worshiper who faced gossip and disloyalty, and they read the heading as placing it in a Davidic collection. Both readings take seriously the combination the psalm describes: serious illness, confessed sin, hostile visitors, and a close friend's treachery.

The closing doxology in verse 13 probably doesn't belong to the psalm's original composition. Most scholars think it was added by the editors who arranged the Psalter into five books, and an old Jewish tradition compares those five books of psalms with the five books of Moses. Whether the editors intended that parallel is debated, but the division itself is marked plainly by the doxologies.
cultural:
Visiting the sick was a social duty in Israel, but verse 6 describes visitors who come to gather gossip, not to comfort. They leave the sickroom and spread the worst they can find. The judgment that the sick man has a vile disease poured into him (verse 8) reflects the common assumption that serious illness was a sign of God's curse, which gave enemies license to write him off.

Sharing bread was one of the strongest bonds in the ancient Near East. To eat at someone's table created an obligation of loyalty; to betray a table companion was a particularly shameful treachery. The gesture of lifting the heel against someone in verse 9 is not certain in meaning. It may picture a horse kicking, a person tripping another, or showing the sole of the foot as an insult (a gesture still considered offensive in many Middle Eastern cultures). Whatever its exact picture, it describes a friend turned attacker. Caring for the poor, praised in verse 1, was a central demand of Israel's law and prophets, and the psalm promises that those who show mercy will receive it.
literary: The psalm has an introduction in the style of wisdom teaching (verses 1 to 3), a lament that quotes the speaker's own prayer and the words of his enemies (verses 4 to 10), a statement of confidence (verses 11 and 12), and the doxology (verse 13). The contrast between the blessed man who considers the poor and the enemies who consider the worst for the sick man sets up the lament. Verses 4 and 10 frame the central section with the same plea, be gracious to me. The enemies' words, quoted in verses 5 and 8, are harsh and final; the psalmist's response in verses 11 and 12 is quiet confidence that God delights in him and has set him in his presence forever.

outline.t: Blessing on the one who cares for the poor
Plea for grace and healing, with confession
Malicious visitors and a friend's betrayal
Raise me up: confidence in God's delight

doctrines.note: Verse 4 combines a plea for healing with confession: heal me, for I have sinned against You. The psalmist doesn't assume innocence, even as he is wronged by others.
The psalm shows how deeply betrayal wounds when it comes from someone who shared one's table. Faithfulness in friendship and household is part of the covenant life God expects of his people.
The closing doxology blesses the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. God's eternity frames every trouble in Book I; he was God before the trouble and will be God after it.

words.note: Sakal, to consider, to act wisely or with insight. In verse 1 it is translated cares for, describing the one who pays thoughtful attention to the poor. The root is the same as the heading Maskil. The blessed person is not simply generous but perceptive, seeing the need and acting wisely.

Aqev, heel. To lift the heel against someone is an image of betrayal or contempt, though its precise picture is debated. The word also plays a part in the story of Jacob, whose name is linked to grasping Esau's heel (Genesis 25:26). Jesus quotes this line about Judas in John 13:18.

Amen, a word of affirmation meaning it is true or so be it, from a root meaning firm or reliable. The double Amen in verse 13 is the congregation's response to the doxology, sealing Book I of the Psalter. The word passed unchanged into Greek and into Christian worship.

christ: At the Last Supper, Jesus quoted verse 9 about the one who shared his bread lifting up his heel against him, applying it to Judas (John 13:18). Jesus uses the psalm as Scripture fulfilled in his betrayal, and it shows that he understood his suffering as part of the pattern of the righteous king betrayed by a trusted companion. Notably, John's quotation leaves out the phrase whom I trusted, which some interpreters think is deliberate: Jesus knew from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64). The psalmist's prayer to be raised up (verse 10) finds its fullest answer in the resurrection. And the psalm's opening blessing on those who care for the poor is echoed in Jesus' teaching that the merciful will be shown mercy (Matthew 5:7).

hard.q: How can the psalmist ask to be raised up so that he may repay his enemies?
hard.a: Verse 10 asks God to raise him up that I may repay them. It sounds like a prayer for revenge. Interpreters answer in different ways. Some, reading the psalm as David's, argue that the king had a duty to restore justice against rebels and traitors, so that repaying them meant restoring order, not personal vengeance. Others see a natural, honest cry of a wronged person that the psalm records without endorsing every desire in it. Still others note that verses 11 and 12 immediately shift the focus: the evidence of God's favor is that the enemy does not triumph, and the psalmist rests in God's presence rather than in revenge. Christians read the verse alongside Jesus' command to love enemies and Paul's instruction to leave vengeance to God (Romans 12:19), while granting that the psalm tells the truth about how betrayal feels.

questions: The psalm pronounces a blessing on those who pay thoughtful attention to the poor. Who is poor or weak around you, and what would considering them wisely look like?
Have you been hurt by someone you trusted? How does it help to know that the Bible, and Jesus himself, knew this kind of betrayal?
Book I ends in praise after so many laments. Why do you think the editors of the Psalter closed each book with a blessing of God?
